description: Identity and Zero Trust for a cloud and platform architect: authentication and assurance, PKI, OAuth 2.0, OIDC, tokens, SAML and legacy federation, authorization models, NIST 800-207 Zero Trust, workload identity (SPIFFE, Kubernetes, cloud federation), cloud IAM patterns and identity threats. Protocol and architecture concepts, not vendor trivia.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::01 Identity Concepts
notes.front: Authentication vs authorization: key difference?
notes.back: Authentication proves who you are (verifying a credential). Authorization decides what you may do. Authn comes first; authz consumes its result.
notes.analogy: Airport: passport control checks who you are (authn); the boarding pass decides which plane you may board (authz).
notes.extra: Pitfall: "401 Unauthorized" is really an authentication failure; 403 Forbidden is the authorization failure.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::01 Identity Concepts
notes.front: Why is an identifier (username, email, sub) not an identity?
notes.back: An identifier is just a label pointing at an identity. Identity is the set of attributes and the proof binding a subject to them.
notes.extra: Pitfall: emails change hands and get reassigned; keying authorization on them instead of a stable sub causes account takeovers.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::01 Identity Concepts
notes.front: What is a credential, as distinct from an identity?
notes.back: Evidence used to prove an identity claim: a password, key, certificate, token. Credentials rotate and expire; the identity persists.
notes.analogy: Your identity is you; your passport is a credential. Renewing the passport doesn't make you a different person.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::01 Identity Concepts
notes.front: What does federation mean in identity?
notes.back: One domain (the identity provider (IdP)) authenticates a user and asserts the result to another domain (the service provider (SP)/relying party (RP)) that trusts it, so users aren't re-registered everywhere.
notes.analogy: A driving licence issued by one state is accepted as ID in another: trust the issuer, don't re-verify the person.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::01 Identity Concepts
notes.text: Federation roles: the {{c1::Identity Provider (IdP)}} authenticates the user and issues assertions; the {{c2::Service Provider (SP) / Relying Party (RP)}} consumes them and grants access.
notes.extra: Naming: Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) says SP; OAuth/OpenID Connect (OIDC) say Relying Party or Client. Same role.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::01 Identity Concepts
notes.front: Relying Party vs Service Provider: different things?
notes.back: Same role, different vocabularies: SP is Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML)'s term, RP is OpenID Connect (OIDC)'s. Both consume an identity assertion from an identity provider (IdP).

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::01 Identity Concepts
notes.front: Single sign-on (SSO) vs federation: how do they relate?
notes.back: Federation is the trust/protocol relationship between identity provider (IdP) and service providers (SPs). SSO is the user experience it enables: one login, many apps.
notes.extra: You can have SSO without federation (one shared session store inside one company) and federation without seamless SSO.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::01 Identity Concepts
notes.front: What is the identity provider (IdP) as a single point of failure trade-off in federation?
notes.back: Central IdP: one place to enforce multi-factor authentication (MFA), revoke, audit. But one outage or compromise affects every federated app at once.
notes.extra: Mitigation: hardened IdP, phishing-resistant admin MFA, monitored break-glass accounts, short sessions.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::01 Identity Concepts
notes.front: What does account linking solve?
notes.back: Mapping several external identities (Google, corporate Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML), local password) to one internal account, so the app has one subject regardless of login route.
notes.extra: Pitfall: auto-linking by email lets an attacker with a matching unverified email at another identity provider (IdP) take over the account.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::01 Identity Concepts
notes.front: Why is linking accounts by an unverified email claim dangerous?
notes.back: An attacker registers at a lax identity provider (IdP) with the victim's email and gets linked to the victim's account: account takeover. Link on iss+sub, or only on verified emails from trusted IdPs.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::01 Identity Concepts
notes.front: In National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) Special Publication (SP) 800-63, what are identity assurance level (IAL), authenticator assurance level (AAL) and federation assurance level (FAL)?
notes.back: Three independent assurance levels: IAL identity proofing, AAL authentication strength, FAL federation assertion protection. Each 1–3.
notes.analogy: Three independent dials on a mixing desk: how well we checked who you are, how strongly you log in, how safely the assertion travels.
notes.extra: Independent on purpose: a well-proofed identity can still log in with a weak authenticator, and vice versa.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::01 Identity Concepts
notes.text: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) 800-63 Identity Assurance Level (IAL): IAL1 = {{c1::self-asserted attributes, no proofing}}; IAL2 = {{c2::remote or in-person proofing against evidence}}; IAL3 = {{c3::in-person (or supervised remote) proofing with physical evidence verification}}.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::01 Identity Concepts
notes.text: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) 800-63 Authenticator Assurance Level (AAL): AAL1 = {{c1::single factor}}; AAL2 = {{c2::two factors (or one multi-factor authenticator)}}; AAL3 = {{c3::hardware-based, verifier-impersonation-resistant authenticator}}.
notes.extra: In practice: authenticator assurance level 3 (AAL3) means Fast IDentity Online 2 (FIDO2) security keys or personal identity verification (PIV) smart cards, not time-based one-time password (TOTP) or push.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::01 Identity Concepts
notes.front: Why does National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) 800-63 separate identity proofing from authentication?
notes.back: Proofing happens once, at enrollment (who is this person?). Authentication happens every login (is this the same subject as enrolled?). Different risks, different controls.
notes.analogy: Proofing is the background check when you're hired; authentication is swiping your badge each morning.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::02 Credentials & Authentication
notes.front: Why store password hashes with a slow key derivation function (KDF) instead of a fast hash like SHA-256?
notes.back: A fast hash lets attackers test billions of guesses per second offline. A deliberately slow, salted, memory-hard KDF makes each guess expensive.
notes.analogy: A lock that takes a second to try each key is fine for the owner but ruins a burglar with a million keys.
notes.extra: Choices: Argon2id (preferred), scrypt, bcrypt. Password-based key derivation function 2 (PBKDF2) only where Federal Information Processing Standards (FIPS) compliance forces it.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::02 Credentials & Authentication
notes.front: What does a salt protect against in password storage?
notes.back: Precomputed (rainbow) tables and cross-user attacks: a unique random salt per password means identical passwords hash differently and each must be cracked separately.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::02 Credentials & Authentication
notes.front: Salt vs pepper in password hashing?
notes.back: Salt: per-user, random, stored beside the hash. Pepper: one secret value kept outside the database (hardware security module (HSM), config) so a DB dump alone can't be cracked.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::02 Credentials & Authentication
notes.front: Why does National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) 800-63B advise against forced periodic password rotation and composition rules?
notes.back: They produce predictable patterns (Summer2024!) and reuse. Better: check against breached-password lists, allow long passphrases, rotate only on evidence of compromise.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::02 Credentials & Authentication
notes.front: What makes an authenticator phishing-resistant?
notes.back: The credential is cryptographically bound to the legitimate origin, so a look-alike site can't obtain a usable response. User judgment is not in the loop.
notes.extra: Phishing-resistant: Fast IDentity Online 2 (FIDO2)/Web Authentication (WebAuthn), personal identity verification (PIV)/smart cards, certificate-based auth. Not: short message service (SMS), time-based one-time password (TOTP), push, email codes.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::02 Credentials & Authentication
notes.front: Why is time-based one-time password (TOTP) phishable even though the code changes every 30 seconds?
notes.back: An attacker-in-the-middle proxy relays the code to the real site within the window. The code proves possession of the seed, not that you're talking to the right site.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::02 Credentials & Authentication
notes.front: Why is short message service (SMS) one-time password (OTP) the weakest second factor?
notes.back: Subscriber identity module (SIM) swapping, Signaling System No. 7 (SS7) interception and phishing relays all defeat it. Possession of a phone number is not strong possession of a device.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::02 Credentials & Authentication
notes.front: What is multi-factor authentication (MFA) fatigue (push bombing), and what counters it?
notes.back: Flooding a user with push prompts until they tap Approve. Counters: number matching, showing location/app context, rate limits, or moving to Fast IDentity Online 2 (FIDO2).
notes.extra: Used in the 2022 Uber breach: the attacker also messaged the victim on WhatsApp pretending to be IT.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::02 Credentials & Authentication
notes.front: Time-based one-time password (TOTP) vs push notification multi-factor authentication (MFA): trade-off?
notes.back: TOTP: offline, no vendor dependency, but typed and phishable. Push: better UX and context, but needs connectivity and invites fatigue attacks. Neither resists adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) phishing.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::02 Credentials & Authentication
notes.front: Passkeys are enrolled, but password + short message service (SMS) one-time password (OTP) remains as a fallback. What does that do to security?
notes.back: The weakest allowed path sets the real strength: an attacker phishes or SIM-swaps the fallback and never meets the phishing-resistant method. Remove or tightly gate fallbacks.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::02 Credentials & Authentication
notes.front: How does Web Authentication (WebAuthn) achieve phishing resistance?
notes.back: The browser includes the site's origin in the signed challenge and the authenticator holds a key pair per origin. A fake domain gets a different key, so the signature never fits.
notes.analogy: A key cut for one specific door: the phishing site has a different lock, so the key simply doesn't turn.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::02 Credentials & Authentication
notes.text: Fast IDentity Online 2 (FIDO2) = {{c1::WebAuthn}} (the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) browser API between site and browser) + {{c2::CTAP}} (the protocol between browser/OS and the external authenticator, e.g. over USB/near-field communication (NFC)/Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE)).

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::02 Credentials & Authentication
notes.front: What is a passkey?
notes.back: A Fast IDentity Online 2 (FIDO2)/Web Authentication (WebAuthn) discoverable credential, usually synced across a user's devices via the platform's cloud keychain, replacing the password entirely.
notes.extra: Trade-off: synced passkeys are convenient but tie assurance to the cloud account; device-bound passkeys (security keys) suit authenticator assurance level 3 (AAL3).

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::02 Credentials & Authentication
notes.front: Roaming vs platform authenticator in Fast IDentity Online 2 (FIDO2)?
notes.back: Roaming: separate hardware (YubiKey) used over Client to Authenticator Protocol (CTAP), portable across devices. Platform: built into the device (Touch ID, Windows Hello, trusted platform module (TPM)-backed).

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::02 Credentials & Authentication
notes.front: In Web Authentication (WebAuthn), what does the Relying Party ID (rpId) constrain?
notes.back: The domain a credential is scoped to. The browser only offers the credential on that domain or its subdomains, which is the heart of the phishing resistance.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::02 Credentials & Authentication
notes.front: Why does a Web Authentication (WebAuthn) biometric not leave the device, and why does that matter for privacy?
notes.back: The biometric only unlocks the local private key. The server sees a signature, never fingerprint data, so a server breach leaks no biometrics.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::02 Credentials & Authentication
notes.front: Why does step-up authentication exist?
notes.back: Not every action deserves the same friction. Log in at a low level; demand a stronger factor only for sensitive operations (payments, admin changes).
notes.extra: OpenID Connect (OIDC) expresses it with acr_values requests and the acr claim in the ID token.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::03 PKI & Certificates
notes.front: What does an X.509 certificate actually assert?
notes.back: A CA's signed statement: "this public key belongs to this subject (name/subject alternative name (SAN)), valid for this period, for these usages." It binds a key to an identity.
notes.analogy: A notarised letter: the notary (CA) vouches that the signature (public key) belongs to the named person.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::03 PKI & Certificates
notes.front: A server presents a chain that validates to a trusted root, but its hostname is not in the Subject Alternative Name (SAN). What happens, and why?
notes.back: Clients reject it with a name mismatch. A valid chain proves who signed the certificate, but the SAN is what binds the key to the name the client asked for.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::03 PKI & Certificates
notes.front: How does a certificate chain establish trust?
notes.back: Each certificate is signed by the one above; the chain ends at a root in the verifier's trust store. Trusting the root means trusting everything it signed.
notes.extra: Pitfall: servers forgetting to send intermediates; clients can't build the chain and fail with 'unknown issuer'.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::03 PKI & Certificates
notes.front: Why do certificate authorities (CAs) use offline roots and online intermediates?
notes.back: The root key is the crown jewel: keep it offline and sign rarely. Intermediates do daily issuance; if one is compromised, revoke it without replacing every trust store.
notes.analogy: The master key stays in a vault; staff carry sub-keys that can be re-cut if lost.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::03 PKI & Certificates
notes.front: What is a trust store, and why do different clients disagree about validity?
notes.back: The set of root certificate authorities (CAs) a verifier accepts. Browsers, OSes, Java and containers ship different stores, so one cert may validate in Chrome and fail in a Java virtual machine (JVM) or Alpine image.
notes.analogy: The list of notaries your bank recognises: a perfectly genuine stamp from an unlisted notary is still rejected.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::03 PKI & Certificates
notes.front: What is a CSR, and what does it deliberately not contain?
notes.back: A Certificate Signing Request: the public key plus requested subject/subject alternative names (SANs), signed with the private key to prove possession. The private key never leaves the requester.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::03 PKI & Certificates
notes.text: Certificate name matching: modern clients check the {{c1::Subject Alternative Name (SAN)}} extension, not the legacy {{c2::Common Name (CN)}} field, which browsers now ignore.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::03 PKI & Certificates
notes.front: What do Key Usage and Extended Key Usage constrain?
notes.back: What a certificate's key may do (signing, key encipherment, certificate authority (CA) signing) and for which purposes (serverAuth, clientAuth, codeSigning). A server cert shouldn't sign other certs.
notes.extra: Pitfall: service-mesh client auth failing because a cert lacks clientAuth EKU.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::03 PKI & Certificates
notes.front: What does the Basic Constraints: certificate authority (CA) flag prevent?
notes.back: A leaf certificate acting as an issuer. Without the check, anyone with a valid server cert could mint certificates for any domain.
notes.extra: This was a real bug class in early browsers and in some TLS libraries that skipped the check.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::03 PKI & Certificates
notes.front: Why is revocation the weakest part of public key infrastructure (PKI)?
notes.back: The cert looks valid until it expires; the verifier must actively ask whether it was revoked. Certificate revocation lists (CRLs) lag and grow; Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) adds latency, privacy leaks and soft-fail.
notes.analogy: A stolen credit card still has a valid expiry date printed on it; only a live check with the bank reveals the block.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::03 PKI & Certificates
notes.front: What is Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) soft-fail, and why does it undermine revocation?
notes.back: If the OCSP responder is unreachable, most clients proceed as if valid. An attacker who can block OCSP traffic therefore neutralises revocation.
notes.analogy: A guard who waves everyone through whenever the phone line to headquarters is dead.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::03 PKI & Certificates
notes.front: What is Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) Must-Staple meant to fix?
notes.back: Soft-fail: the certificate declares that a stapled OCSP response is required, so a missing staple is treated as failure instead of silently passing.
notes.extra: Rarely deployed; the industry is moving to short-lived certificates and browser-pushed revocation lists (CRLite, CRLSets) instead.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::03 PKI & Certificates
notes.front: Why do short-lived certificates change the revocation problem rather than solve it?
notes.back: With hours-to-days validity, expiry does the revoking: no certificate revocation list (CRL)/Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) needed. The cost moves to issuance automation, which must now be highly available.
notes.analogy: A day pass instead of a lifetime membership you would otherwise have to cancel.
notes.extra: Trade-off: an issuance outage now becomes an availability outage within hours.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::03 PKI & Certificates
notes.front: What does Automatic Certificate Management Environment (ACME) automate?
notes.back: Domain validation and certificate issuance/renewal between a client and a certificate authority (CA): prove control of the name via an HTTP or DNS challenge, receive a cert, repeat before expiry.
notes.extra: Made famous by Let's Encrypt; cert-manager uses it in Kubernetes.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::03 PKI & Certificates
notes.front: Automatic Certificate Management Environment (ACME) HTTP-01 vs DNS-01 challenge: when do you need DNS-01?
notes.back: HTTP-01 serves a token on port 80 of the host. DNS-01 publishes a TXT record and is the only option for wildcard certs or hosts not reachable from the internet.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::03 PKI & Certificates
notes.text: Certificate lifecycle: {{c1::key generation}} → {{c2::CSR}} → {{c3::validation (domain/organisation)}} → {{c4::issuance}} → deployment → {{c5::renewal or revocation}}. Automate every step or outages follow.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::03 PKI & Certificates
notes.front: Why do certificate expiries cause so many outages?
notes.back: Issuance is automated once, renewal is forgotten; hidden certs (internal certificate authorities (CAs), mutual TLS (mTLS) clients, webhooks) have no owner and no monitoring until they expire.
notes.analogy: Smoke-detector batteries: everyone knows they expire, nobody owns the calendar.
notes.extra: In practice: inventory every cert, alert on expiry, and prefer short lifetimes so renewal breakage surfaces early and often.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::03 PKI & Certificates
notes.front: What does Certificate Transparency add to public public key infrastructure (PKI)?
notes.back: Public, append-only logs of every issued cert. Mis-issuance becomes detectable by the domain owner instead of relying on certificate authorities (CAs) behaving.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::04 OAuth 2.0
notes.front: What problem does OAuth 2.0 solve?
notes.back: Delegated authorization: let a client app access a user's resources at an API without the user handing over their password to the client.
notes.analogy: A hotel key card: it opens your room for your stay, but you never give the guest your master key or your identity.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::04 OAuth 2.0
notes.text: OAuth 2.0 roles: {{c1::Resource Owner}} (the user), {{c2::Client}} (the app wanting access), {{c3::Authorization Server}} (issues tokens), {{c4::Resource Server}} (the API that accepts tokens).

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::04 OAuth 2.0
notes.front: Confidential vs public client in OAuth?
notes.back: Confidential clients (server-side apps) can keep a client secret. Public clients (single-page applications (SPAs), mobile, CLI) cannot, so they must use Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE) and never rely on a secret.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::04 OAuth 2.0
notes.front: Why does the authorization code flow exchange a code for a token instead of returning the token directly?
notes.back: The code travels through the browser (front channel) and is useless without the client's back-channel exchange. Tokens never touch the browser URL, history or logs.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::04 OAuth 2.0
notes.front: List every step of the OAuth authorization code flow with Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE) and what each step protects against.
notes.back: 1. Client makes a random code_verifier and sends its hash (code_challenge) plus state via the browser. 2. User authenticates and consents at the authorization server (AS). 3. AS redirects back with a code (checked against state: stops forged callbacks). 4. Client sends code + verifier over the back channel (verifier stops a stolen code being used). 5. AS returns tokens directly, never via the URL.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::04 OAuth 2.0
notes.text: Authorization code flow: client redirects user to the authorization server (AS)'s {{c1::authorization endpoint}} → user authenticates/consents → AS redirects back with a {{c2::code}} → client POSTs code to the {{c3::token endpoint}} → receives access (and refresh) token.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::04 OAuth 2.0
notes.front: Front channel vs back channel in OAuth?
notes.back: Front channel: messages via browser redirects, visible and tamperable. Back channel: direct server-to-server HTTPS call. Secrets and tokens belong on the back channel.
notes.analogy: Front channel: a note carried by the user through a crowded hall. Back channel: a sealed phone line between two offices.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::04 OAuth 2.0
notes.front: What attack does Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE) prevent?
notes.back: Authorization code interception: a malicious app on the same device steals the code from the redirect. Without the original code_verifier the stolen code is worthless.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::04 OAuth 2.0
notes.front: A malicious app on the same device steals the authorization code from the redirect. Why can't it get a token when Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE) is used?
notes.back: The token endpoint demands the original code_verifier. The attacker saw only the code (and at most the hash, code_challenge), and a hash cannot be reversed to the verifier.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::04 OAuth 2.0
notes.text: Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE): client generates a random {{c1::code_verifier}}, sends its SHA-256 hash as {{c2::code_challenge}} with the authorization request, then presents the verifier at the token endpoint; the authorization server (AS) re-hashes and compares.
notes.analogy: Send a sealed photo of your key first; later show the key itself and prove it matches the photo.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::04 OAuth 2.0
notes.front: Why is the implicit grant deprecated?
notes.back: The access token is returned in the URL fragment: exposed to browser history, referrers and scripts, with no client authentication and no way to use Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE).
notes.extra: Replacement: authorization code + PKCE, even for single-page applications (SPAs).

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::04 OAuth 2.0
notes.front: Why is Resource Owner Password Credentials (ROPC) deprecated?
notes.back: The client handles the user's password, defeating OAuth's purpose, and it can't support multi-factor authentication (MFA), single sign-on (SSO) or phishing-resistant login.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::04 OAuth 2.0
notes.front: When is the client credentials grant the right choice?
notes.back: Machine-to-machine calls with no user involved: the client authenticates as itself to the token endpoint and gets a token representing the application.
notes.extra: Pitfall: using it for user-facing actions hides the real actor from audit logs.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::04 OAuth 2.0
notes.front: What is the device authorization grant for?
notes.back: Input-constrained devices (TVs, CLIs): the device shows a short code and URL, the user approves on a phone, and the device polls the token endpoint.
notes.extra: Risk: device-code phishing; attackers send victims a legitimate verification URL and code to approve.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::04 OAuth 2.0
notes.front: What is a refresh token, and why separate it from the access token?
notes.back: A long-lived credential used only at the token endpoint to obtain new short-lived access tokens. Keeps access tokens short without forcing re-login.
notes.analogy: Access token = daily visitor badge; refresh token = the letter at reception that lets you collect a new badge each morning.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::04 OAuth 2.0
notes.front: What is refresh token rotation, and what does it detect?
notes.back: Each refresh returns a new refresh token and invalidates the old one. If a stolen old token is replayed, the authorization server (AS) detects reuse and revokes the whole family.
notes.analogy: A ticket stub torn at every use; if two people show the same stub number, the whole ticket is voided.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::04 OAuth 2.0
notes.front: What does an OAuth scope express?
notes.back: The client's requested permissions at the resource server (read:repo). Scopes limit the client, not what the user may do: both constraints apply.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::04 OAuth 2.0
notes.front: Scope vs audience in an access token?
notes.back: Scope: what operations are allowed. Audience: which resource server the token is for. A token with the right scope but wrong audience must be rejected.
notes.analogy: Scope is what the ticket lets you do; audience is which venue it's valid at.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::04 OAuth 2.0
notes.front: Why must the authorization server (AS) validate the redirect_uri with exact string matching?
notes.back: Pattern or prefix matching lets an attacker register or craft a uniform resource identifier (URI) that sends the authorization code to a server they control (open-redirect to code theft).

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::04 OAuth 2.0
notes.front: What is the state parameter for?
notes.back: Cross-site request forgery (CSRF) protection on the redirect: the client binds a random value to the user's session and checks it on return, so an attacker can't inject their own code into your session.
notes.analogy: A cloakroom tag: you only accept the coat handed back if the number matches the tag in your pocket.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::04 OAuth 2.0
notes.front: What attack becomes possible if a client skips checking the state value on the callback?
notes.back: Login cross-site request forgery (CSRF): the attacker sends the victim a callback carrying the attacker's own code, so the victim's session becomes linked to the attacker's account.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::04 OAuth 2.0
notes.front: What does OAuth 2.1 change versus 2.0?
notes.back: Consolidates the security best current practice (BCP): Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE) required, implicit and resource owner password credentials (ROPC) removed, exact redirect uniform resource identifier (URI) matching, refresh tokens sender-constrained or rotated, no bearer tokens in query strings.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::04 OAuth 2.0
notes.front: Why are bearer tokens risky by design?
notes.back: Whoever holds the token can use it; there is no proof the presenter is the legitimate client. Theft equals access until expiry.
notes.analogy: Cash: whoever holds the note can spend it, no questions asked.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::05 OpenID Connect
notes.front: What does OpenID Connect add on top of OAuth 2.0?
notes.back: An identity layer: a signed ID token saying who authenticated, when and how, plus standard claims, discovery and a userinfo endpoint.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::05 OpenID Connect
notes.front: Which question does OAuth 2.0 answer, and which does OpenID Connect (OIDC) answer?
notes.back: OAuth: "may this client call that API on the user's behalf?" (authorization). OIDC: "who just authenticated, and how?" (authentication, via the ID token).

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::05 OpenID Connect
notes.front: ID token vs access token: who is each for?
notes.back: ID token: for the client, proves the user authenticated. Access token: for the resource server, grants API access. Never send an ID token to an API as authorization.
notes.analogy: ID token = your passport, shown to the app. Access token = the boarding pass, shown at the gate (the API).

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::05 OpenID Connect
notes.front: Why must an API not accept an ID token as an access token?
notes.back: Its audience is the client, not the API; it carries no scopes and may contain personally identifiable information (PII). Accepting it lets any client that received an ID token call your API.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::05 OpenID Connect
notes.text: Core ID-token claims: iss = {{c1::issuer}}; sub = {{c2::stable subject identifier}}; aud = {{c3::client ID it was issued to}}; exp = {{c4::expiry}}; iat = {{c5::issued-at}}; nonce = {{c6::replay binding to the request}}.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::05 OpenID Connect
notes.front: Which ID-token claim should you key user accounts on, and why not email?
notes.back: sub (scoped to iss). Emails can change or be reassigned; some identity providers (IdPs) don't verify them. iss+sub is the stable, unique pair.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::05 OpenID Connect
notes.front: What is the nonce in OpenID Connect (OIDC) for?
notes.back: The client puts a random nonce in the authentication request; the identity provider (IdP) echoes it in the ID token. The client verifies it to tie the token to its own request and block replay.
notes.extra: vs state: state protects the redirect/session (CSRF); nonce protects the ID token itself.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::05 OpenID Connect
notes.front: state vs nonce: how to tell them apart?
notes.back: state: OAuth, round-trips via the redirect, binds the response to the browser session. nonce: OpenID Connect (OIDC), lands inside the signed ID token, binds the token to the request.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::05 OpenID Connect
notes.front: What does OpenID Connect (OIDC) Discovery provide?
notes.back: A JSON document at /.well-known/openid-configuration listing endpoints, supported scopes/algorithms and the jwks_uri, so clients configure themselves from the issuer URL alone.
notes.analogy: A phone book published at a well-known address: give me the issuer, I look up every number myself.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::05 OpenID Connect
notes.front: What is the userinfo endpoint, and when would you use it instead of ID-token claims?
notes.back: An OAuth-protected endpoint returning the user's claims for an access token. Use it when the ID token is kept minimal or when claims change during the session.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::05 OpenID Connect
notes.text: OpenID Connect (OIDC) standard scopes: openid = {{c1::required; requests an ID token}}; profile = {{c2::name, picture and similar claims}}; email = {{c3::email address claims}}; offline_access = {{c4::asks for a refresh token}}.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::05 OpenID Connect
notes.front: What do the acr and amr claims tell a relying party?
notes.back: acr: the authentication context class (assurance level) achieved. amr: the methods used (pwd, otp, hwk). Both let RPs enforce step-up policy.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::05 OpenID Connect
notes.front: OpenID Connect (OIDC) response_type: what does code vs id_token vs hybrid mean?
notes.back: code: everything via back-channel (recommended). id_token: implicit, token in the fragment (deprecated). Hybrid (code id_token): ID token up front, access token via code.
notes.extra: Modern guidance: just use code with Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE); hybrid's benefit (early identity) rarely justifies the complexity.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::05 OpenID Connect
notes.front: What are OpenID Connect (OIDC) front-channel and back-channel logout?
notes.back: Ways for the identity provider (IdP) to tell relying parties (RPs) a session ended: front-channel via hidden iframes in the browser; back-channel via a signed logout token POSTed server-to-server (more reliable).

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::05 OpenID Connect
notes.front: Why is single logout so hard in federated systems?
notes.back: Each relying party (RP) holds its own session; the identity provider (IdP) must notify every one, over channels that may fail. Short RP sessions plus continuous revalidation are more robust than perfect logout.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::05 OpenID Connect
notes.front: OpenID Connect (OIDC) vs Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML): how to tell them apart at a glance?
notes.back: OIDC: JSON/JSON Web Token (JWT) over REST, built on OAuth, mobile and API friendly. SAML: Extensible Markup Language (XML) assertions via browser POST, enterprise single sign-on (SSO), no API access story.
notes.extra: Rule of thumb: new apps and anything calling APIs → OIDC; legacy enterprise SaaS integration → SAML.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::05 OpenID Connect
notes.front: When should an architect still choose Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) over OpenID Connect (OIDC)?
notes.back: When the partner or SaaS only supports SAML, or an existing enterprise identity provider (IdP) and compliance tooling is built around SAML attribute contracts.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::06 Tokens: JWT, Opaque & Introspection
notes.text: A JSON Web Signature (JWS)-style JSON Web Token (JWT) has three Base64url parts: the header holds {{c1::alg, kid, typ}}; the payload holds {{c2::the claims}}; the signature is computed over {{c3::the header and payload}}.
notes.extra: Pitfall: Base64url is encoding, not encryption. Anyone can read the payload; only JSON Web Encryption (JWE) encrypts it.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::06 Tokens: JWT, Opaque & Introspection
notes.front: JSON Web Signature (JWS) vs JSON Web Encryption (JWE)?
notes.back: JWS: signed JSON Web Token (JWT), readable by anyone, integrity and origin guaranteed. JWE: encrypted JWT, contents hidden from the client. Most access/ID tokens are JWS.
notes.analogy: JWS is a postcard with a tamper-evident seal; JWE is a sealed envelope.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::06 Tokens: JWT, Opaque & Introspection
notes.front: Self-contained (JWT) vs opaque access tokens: trade-off?
notes.back: JWT: validated locally with the issuer's public key, fast, but can't be revoked before expiry. Opaque: just a reference, must be introspected, but revocation is immediate.
notes.analogy: JWT = a signed letter you can read yourself; opaque token = a claim ticket you must hand to the counter.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::06 Tokens: JWT, Opaque & Introspection
notes.front: A fired employee holds a JSON Web Token (JWT) access token with 1 hour left. What can they still do, and how do you limit it?
notes.back: Any resource server validating locally still accepts it until exp. Limit with short lifetimes, refresh-token revocation, introspection for sensitive APIs, or push revocation events.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::06 Tokens: JWT, Opaque & Introspection
notes.front: What is token introspection?
notes.back: A resource server POSTs a token to the authorization server (AS)'s introspection endpoint and gets back active plus claims. Needed for opaque tokens; optional for JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) when you want live revocation.
notes.analogy: Phoning the issuing bank to ask whether the card is still active before accepting it.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::06 Tokens: JWT, Opaque & Introspection
notes.front: Why is the alg: none JSON Web Token (JWT) attack possible?
notes.back: Libraries that trust the header's alg treat an unsigned token as valid. Verifiers must pin the expected algorithm and reject none.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::06 Tokens: JWT, Opaque & Introspection
notes.front: What is the RSA with SHA-256 (RS256)-to-HMAC with SHA-256 (HS256) key confusion attack?
notes.back: Attacker switches alg to hash-based message authentication code (HMAC) and signs with the server's public key as the HMAC secret. A library that accepts any alg verifies it successfully.
notes.extra: Defence: fix allowed algorithms per key; never let the token choose.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::06 Tokens: JWT, Opaque & Introspection
notes.text: Mandatory JSON Web Token (JWT) checks: signature with the expected key; iss {{c1::equals the trusted issuer}}; aud {{c2::contains this service}}; exp {{c3::has not passed (allow small clock skew)}}; nbf {{c4::has been reached, if present}}.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::06 Tokens: JWT, Opaque & Introspection
notes.front: Why must a resource server check aud even when the signature is valid?
notes.back: A valid token for another API from the same issuer would otherwise be accepted. Audience restriction stops token reuse across services (confused deputy).

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::06 Tokens: JWT, Opaque & Introspection
notes.front: What does a Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) AudienceRestriction prevent?
notes.back: An assertion issued for service provider (SP) A being replayed at SP B. Each SP must reject assertions whose audience is not its own entity ID.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::06 Tokens: JWT, Opaque & Introspection
notes.front: What does the kid header do, and what's its security pitfall?
notes.back: Selects which key from the issuer's key set verifies the token, enabling rotation. Pitfall: treating kid as a file path or SQL value (injection) or fetching keys from a URL in the token.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::06 Tokens: JWT, Opaque & Introspection
notes.front: What is a JWKS endpoint, and how does it enable key rotation?
notes.back: A JSON Web Key Set of the issuer's current public keys. The issuer publishes a new key, signs with it after a grace period, and verifiers fetch by kid; old keys retire later.
notes.analogy: A noticeboard of currently valid official stamps; verifiers compare the stamp on a letter to the board.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::06 Tokens: JWT, Opaque & Introspection
notes.front: What is the jku / x5u header pitfall?
notes.back: They let the token name a URL for its own verification key. A verifier that follows it accepts attacker-hosted keys. Only trust keys from the pre-configured issuer.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::06 Tokens: JWT, Opaque & Introspection
notes.front: What is a sender-constrained (proof-of-possession) token?
notes.back: A token bound to a key the client must prove it holds (Demonstrating Proof-of-Possession (DPoP) or mutual TLS (mTLS)). A stolen token alone is useless without the key.
notes.analogy: A cheque payable only to the named account holder, versus cash.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::06 Tokens: JWT, Opaque & Introspection
notes.front: How does Demonstrating Proof-of-Possession (DPoP) work in one sentence?
notes.back: The client signs each HTTP request (method, URL, time, token hash) with a private key whose public part the authorization server (AS) bound to the token; the resource server (RS) verifies both.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::06 Tokens: JWT, Opaque & Introspection
notes.front: Demonstrating Proof-of-Possession (DPoP) vs mutual TLS (mTLS)-bound tokens: when to pick which?
notes.back: mTLS binding (Request for Comments (RFC) 8705) suits services with a cert infrastructure and TLS terminating at the app. DPoP works at the application layer through proxies, content delivery networks (CDNs) and in browsers.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::06 Tokens: JWT, Opaque & Introspection
notes.front: What does OAuth Token Exchange (Request for Comments (RFC) 8693) let a service do?
notes.back: Trade one token for another at the authorization server (AS): narrow scope, change audience for a downstream API, or carry delegation (act claim) so the chain of actors is visible.
notes.extra: Solves the 'pass the user's token everywhere' anti-pattern in microservices.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::06 Tokens: JWT, Opaque & Introspection
notes.front: Impersonation vs delegation in token exchange?
notes.back: Impersonation: the new token looks like it's the user; the intermediary vanishes. Delegation: the token says subject = user, act = service, preserving the audit trail.
notes.analogy: Signing a letter as the boss, versus signing it 'p.p.' on the boss's behalf: delegation keeps your name on it.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::06 Tokens: JWT, Opaque & Introspection
notes.front: Why is token revocation inherently a trade-off against statelessness?
notes.back: Instant revocation needs shared state checked per request; stateless JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) avoid that but stay valid until exp. Short lifetimes plus refresh rotation is the usual compromise.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::06 Tokens: JWT, Opaque & Introspection
notes.front: What is the phantom token (or split token) pattern?
notes.back: Opaque tokens outside, JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) inside: the API gateway introspects or exchanges the opaque token once and forwards a JWT to internal services.
notes.extra: Keeps personally identifiable information (PII) out of clients and gives internal services fast local validation.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::07 SAML & Legacy Federation
notes.front: What is a Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) assertion?
notes.back: A signed Extensible Markup Language (XML) statement from the identity provider (IdP) about a subject: authentication statement (how/when), attribute statement (groups, email), and conditions (audience, validity window).

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::07 SAML & Legacy Federation
notes.text: Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) assertion parts: {{c1::Authentication statement}} (who, when, how); {{c2::Attribute statement}} (name, groups, roles); {{c3::Conditions}} (NotBefore/NotOnOrAfter, AudienceRestriction).

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::07 SAML & Legacy Federation
notes.front: Service provider (SP)-initiated vs identity provider (IdP)-initiated Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) flow?
notes.back: SP-initiated: user hits the app, is redirected to the IdP with an AuthnRequest, returns with a response. IdP-initiated: user clicks the app in the IdP portal; the IdP posts an unsolicited assertion.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::07 SAML & Legacy Federation
notes.front: Why is identity provider (IdP)-initiated Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) considered less secure?
notes.back: No request to bind the response to (no InResponseTo), so stolen assertions can be replayed and attackers can inject a victim into their own session.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::07 SAML & Legacy Federation
notes.front: What does the HTTP-POST binding in Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) mean, and why not a redirect?
notes.back: The assertion is sent as a form field auto-submitted by the browser. Signed Extensible Markup Language (XML) is too large for URL query strings, where redirects would carry it.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::07 SAML & Legacy Federation
notes.front: What is the Extensible Markup Language (XML) Signature Wrapping class of attacks?
notes.back: Moving the signed assertion elsewhere in the document and inserting a forged one where the parser looks. Verifier checks the signature on one node, processes another.
notes.extra: Lesson: XML-DSig's flexibility is the root cause; OpenID Connect (OIDC)'s compact JSON Web Signature (JWS) avoids this class entirely.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::07 SAML & Legacy Federation
notes.front: What is Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) metadata for?
notes.back: An Extensible Markup Language (XML) document each side publishes with entity ID, endpoints, bindings and signing certs, so identity provider (IdP) and service provider (SP) configure trust by exchanging files instead of hand-typing.
notes.analogy: Exchanging business cards with every address, phone number and signature specimen printed on them.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::07 SAML & Legacy Federation
notes.front: What is the NameID in Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML), and what is the persistent vs transient distinction?
notes.back: The subject identifier. Persistent: stable pairwise pseudonym per service provider (SP). Transient: one-time, for anonymous access. Email-format NameIDs are common but unstable.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::07 SAML & Legacy Federation
notes.front: Why does Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) persist despite OpenID Connect (OIDC)?
notes.back: Thousands of enterprise SaaS apps and identity providers (IdPs) already speak it, attribute contracts are embedded in compliance processes, and it works fine for browser single sign-on (SSO).

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::07 SAML & Legacy Federation
notes.front: What does Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) lack that pushed APIs and mobile to OAuth/OpenID Connect (OIDC)?
notes.back: No access-token concept for calling APIs, no native mobile flow, and Extensible Markup Language (XML) parsing is heavy. It only answers "who logged in", not "may this app call that API".

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::07 SAML & Legacy Federation
notes.front: What core idea makes Kerberos different from token-based web federation?
notes.back: Symmetric-key tickets issued by a trusted key distribution center (KDC): tickets are encrypted for a specific service with that service's key, so services verify them without calling home.
notes.analogy: A sealed envelope only the destination can open, issued by a trusted post office.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::07 SAML & Legacy Federation
notes.front: Why doesn't Kerberos work well across the internet or between organisations?
notes.back: It assumes a shared key distribution center (KDC), pre-registered service principals and reachable ports; cross-realm trust is manual. Federation protocols were built for exactly those gaps.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::07 SAML & Legacy Federation
notes.front: Kerberos ticket vs OAuth access token: key contrast?
notes.back: Ticket: symmetric crypto, service-specific, verified offline with the service's own key. Access token: usually asymmetric signature or introspection, HTTP-native, works across organisations.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::07 SAML & Legacy Federation
notes.front: Why does Kerberos require roughly synchronised clocks?
notes.back: Authenticators carry timestamps that the service checks against a small allowed skew to reject replayed ones, so badly skewed clocks make valid logins fail.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::07 SAML & Legacy Federation
notes.front: What is Kerberos delegation, and why is unconstrained delegation dangerous?
notes.back: Letting a service act as the user toward another service. Unconstrained delegation stores the user's ticket-granting ticket (TGT) on the service; compromise it and you are every user who logged in.
notes.extra: Modern analogue: OAuth token exchange with explicit act claims and audience limits.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::07 SAML & Legacy Federation
notes.front: What is Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP), and what role does it still play?
notes.back: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) is a protocol for querying hierarchical directories (users, groups, attributes). Still the backing store behind many identity providers (IdPs) and the authn/authz source for legacy apps.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::07 SAML & Legacy Federation
notes.front: What is an Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) bind, and why is 'authenticate by binding' a weak pattern?
notes.back: A bind authenticates the connection with a distinguished name (DN) and password. Apps that log users in by binding handle plaintext passwords and bypass multi-factor authentication (MFA) and central session control.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::07 SAML & Legacy Federation
notes.front: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) directory vs identity provider (IdP): how to keep them apart?
notes.back: LDAP answers "what attributes does this object have?" over a persistent connection. An IdP answers "did this user authenticate?" with a signed assertion.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::08 Authorization Models
notes.front: What is RBAC, and what is its structural weakness?
notes.back: Permissions attach to roles; subjects get roles. Weakness: role explosion as every combination of context (region, project, team) needs its own role.
notes.analogy: A key ring: fine for a few doors, but soon you carry a separate key for every room in every building.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::08 Authorization Models
notes.front: What is attribute-based access control (ABAC), and what does it solve that RBAC can't?
notes.back: Attribute-based access control (ABAC): policies evaluate attributes of subject, resource, action and environment ("owners may edit their own documents during business hours"). Context without role explosion.
notes.analogy: RBAC is a guest list; ABAC is a bouncer with rules (over 18, dress code, before midnight).

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::08 Authorization Models
notes.front: RBAC vs attribute-based access control (ABAC): how to decide?
notes.back: RBAC when permissions are coarse and stable and auditors want a reviewable role list. ABAC when decisions depend on resource or context attributes. Most systems blend them.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::08 Authorization Models
notes.front: A rule says: "managers approve expenses under 10,000 only in their own region". Why is this awkward in role-based access control (RBAC) and natural in attribute-based access control (ABAC)?
notes.back: RBAC needs a separate role per region and limit combination (role explosion). ABAC states one policy over attributes: user.region == expense.region, amount < 10000, user.title == manager.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::08 Authorization Models
notes.front: What is ReBAC?
notes.back: Relationship-based access control: permissions derive from a graph of relations (user → member of → team → owns → folder → contains → doc). Google Zanzibar popularised it.
notes.analogy: Permissions flow along the branches of an org chart or family tree: you inherit what the folder above you grants.
notes.extra: Suits sharing and hierarchy: Drive, GitHub repos, folder trees.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::08 Authorization Models
notes.front: What problem did Zanzibar solve at Google scale?
notes.back: Consistent, low-latency authorization checks across trillions of relationship tuples with a zookie consistency token to avoid the "new enemy" problem.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::08 Authorization Models
notes.front: What is the new enemy problem in distributed authorization?
notes.back: Stale replica reads: you remove Bob's access then add a document; a check against an old snapshot still grants Bob. Zanzibar's zookies pin checks to a minimum snapshot.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::08 Authorization Models
notes.text: Externalised authorization roles: Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) {{c1::intercepts the request}}; Policy Decision Point (PDP) {{c2::evaluates policy}}; Policy Information Point (PIP) {{c3::supplies attributes}}; Policy Administration Point (PAP) {{c4::authors policies}}.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::08 Authorization Models
notes.front: Policy enforcement point (PEP) vs policy decision point (PDP): key difference?
notes.back: The PEP sits in the request path and enforces (gateway, sidecar, middleware). The PDP decides and knows no HTTP; it can be a library, sidecar or central service.
notes.analogy: PEP is the bouncer at the door; PDP is the manager on the radio who says yes or no.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::08 Authorization Models
notes.front: Why separate the policy decision point (PDP) from the application?
notes.back: Policies change on a different cadence from code, must be auditable by non-developers, and should be consistent across dozens of services.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::08 Authorization Models
notes.front: Cedar vs Rego: what does Cedar prioritise?
notes.back: Cedar (AWS) is purpose-built for authorization: entity/relationship schema, forbid-overrides-permit, analysable and formally verified. Rego is a general query language.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::08 Authorization Models
notes.front: Why do policy engines favour default deny with forbid overriding permit?
notes.back: A forgotten rule fails closed, and a single explicit prohibition can't be undone by accumulating permits elsewhere. It keeps reasoning about policy local.
notes.analogy: A door that locks when the power fails, rather than swinging open.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::08 Authorization Models
notes.front: What is the principle of least privilege in operational terms?
notes.back: Grant the minimum permissions needed for the task, for the minimum time, and remove them when the task ends. It's a process, not a one-time configuration.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::08 Authorization Models
notes.front: Why does decision caching at the policy enforcement point (PEP) need care?
notes.back: Cached allows outlive revocations; cached denies outlive grants. Cache with short time-to-live values (TTLs) keyed on all decision inputs, and invalidate on policy or attribute change.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::08 Authorization Models
notes.front: Coarse-grained vs fine-grained authorization: where does each live?
notes.back: Coarse (may this app/role reach this service?) at the gateway or mesh. Fine (may this user edit this row?) needs resource data, so it lives in or beside the application.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::08 Authorization Models
notes.front: What does separation of duties require of an authorization model?
notes.back: That some permission combinations are forbidden for one subject (request and approve a payment). Needs policy that reasons about toxic combinations, not just grants.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::08 Authorization Models
notes.front: Permissions on identity vs permissions on resource (resource policies)?
notes.back: Identity-based: attached to the subject ("Alice may read bucket X"). Resource-based: attached to the object ("bucket X allows Alice"). Cloud providers evaluate both and intersect them.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::09 Zero Trust Architecture
notes.front: What does Zero Trust reject, in one sentence?
notes.back: The idea that network location implies trust: being inside the perimeter (virtual private network (VPN), office local area network (LAN)) grants nothing; every request is authenticated and authorized on its own.
notes.analogy: A hotel where every door, lift and gym needs your key card, instead of one lobby guard and open corridors.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::09 Zero Trust Architecture
notes.front: Why did the perimeter model fail?
notes.back: Cloud, SaaS, remote work and mobile moved users and data outside; attackers who phished one inside device moved laterally freely. The perimeter protected the wrong boundary.
notes.analogy: Castle and moat: once an attacker is over the wall, every room inside is unlocked.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::09 Zero Trust Architecture
notes.text: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) 800-207 tenets (1–3): all data sources and computing services are {{c1::resources}}; all communication is secured {{c2::regardless of network location}}; access is granted {{c3::per session}}.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::09 Zero Trust Architecture
notes.text: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) 800-207 tenets (4–5): access is determined by {{c1::dynamic policy}} (identity, device, behaviour, environment); the enterprise {{c2::monitors and measures the integrity and security posture}} of all owned assets.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::09 Zero Trust Architecture
notes.text: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) 800-207 tenets (6–7): authentication and authorization are {{c1::dynamic and strictly enforced before access}}; the enterprise {{c2::collects as much information as possible}} about assets and traffic to improve policy.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::09 Zero Trust Architecture
notes.text: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) 800-207 logical components: the {{c1::Policy Engine}} makes the grant/deny decision; the {{c2::Policy Administrator}} establishes or tears down the session path; the {{c3::Policy Enforcement Point}} enables/monitors the connection.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::09 Zero Trust Architecture
notes.front: Policy Engine vs Policy Administrator in National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) 800-207?
notes.back: The Engine decides (trust algorithm over identity, device, risk). The Administrator executes: issues session credentials and tells the policy enforcement point (PEP) to open or close the path.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::09 Zero Trust Architecture
notes.front: Control plane vs data plane in Zero Trust architecture?
notes.back: Control plane: engine and administrator deciding and configuring. Data plane: the policy enforcement point (PEP) and the actual traffic between subject and resource. Decisions are made off-path, enforced in-path.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::09 Zero Trust Architecture
notes.front: What is the implicit trust zone in National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) 800-207?
notes.back: The segment past the policy enforcement point (PEP) where traffic flows without further checks. Zero Trust aims to make that zone as small as possible, ideally a single resource.
notes.analogy: Airside at an airport: past security you walk freely, which is exactly why Zero Trust shrinks that area to one gate.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::09 Zero Trust Architecture
notes.front: What are the three main zero trust architecture (ZTA) deployment approaches in 800-207?
notes.back: Enhanced identity governance (identity is the main policy input), micro-segmentation (network gateways per resource group), and software-defined perimeter (overlay network tunnels).

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::09 Zero Trust Architecture
notes.front: What was BeyondCorp's core move?
notes.back: Google removed virtual private network (VPN) privileges: every internal app was put behind an identity-aware proxy that checked user and device inventory per request, from any network.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::09 Zero Trust Architecture
notes.front: Why does Zero Trust make device identity a first-class input?
notes.back: A legitimate user on a compromised or unmanaged device is still a threat. Device certificates plus posture (patched, disk-encrypted, endpoint detection and response (EDR) running) feed the policy decision.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::09 Zero Trust Architecture
notes.front: An attacker phishes a valid user's password and tries to log in from an unmanaged laptop. Which Zero Trust input stops them even if the credentials are correct?
notes.back: Device identity and posture: no managed-device certificate and no compliant posture means the policy engine denies or limits access, whatever the user credentials say.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::09 Zero Trust Architecture
notes.front: What is device posture?
notes.back: The measurable security state of an endpoint at request time: OS version, disk encryption, endpoint detection and response (EDR) health, jailbreak status. Collected by an agent or mobile device management (MDM) and fed to the policy engine.
notes.analogy: A vehicle inspection sticker checked at the gate: the driver's licence alone doesn't get an unsafe car in.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::09 Zero Trust Architecture
notes.front: What is micro-segmentation in Zero Trust terms?
notes.back: Policy enforcement between individual workloads or small groups (identity-based firewalling, mesh policies), so compromise of one does not grant reach to its neighbours.
notes.analogy: Watertight compartments in a ship: one breach floods one compartment, not the hull.
notes.extra: Differs from virtual local area network (VLAN) segmentation by being identity/workload-aware rather than address-based.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::09 Zero Trust Architecture
notes.front: Zero trust network access (ZTNA) vs virtual private network (VPN): key difference?
notes.back: VPN joins the device to the network (then everything is reachable). ZTNA brokers access to one application at a time after identity and posture checks; the network stays invisible.
notes.analogy: VPN hands you keys to the building; ZTNA escorts you to one specific meeting room each time.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::09 Zero Trust Architecture
notes.front: What is an identity-aware proxy?
notes.back: A reverse proxy that authenticates the user (OpenID Connect (OIDC)/Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML)), checks device and policy, then forwards to the app with identity headers or a signed token. The policy enforcement point (PEP) of BeyondCorp-style zero trust architecture (ZTA).
notes.analogy: A receptionist who checks your ID and your visitor badge, then walks you to one specific office.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::09 Zero Trust Architecture
notes.front: What does continuous evaluation mean in Zero Trust?
notes.back: Trust is re-assessed during the session, not only at login: posture changes, risk signals or revocation events can shorten, step-up or terminate access mid-session.
notes.extra: Standards: Shared Signals Framework / Continuous Access Evaluation Profile (CAEP) let identity providers (IdPs) and apps exchange such events.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::09 Zero Trust Architecture
notes.front: What is the trust algorithm in National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) 800-207?
notes.back: The policy engine's logic combining subject identity, device, resource sensitivity, behaviour and threat intel into a decision; may be score-based or criteria-based, singular or contextual.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::10 Workload & Machine Identity
notes.front: Why do workloads need identities rather than shared secrets?
notes.back: Secrets are static, copied, leaked in logs and hard to rotate. An identity is attested from the platform, short-lived and specific to one workload, so it can be authorized and audited.
notes.analogy: A shared door code versus a named badge: the code tells you nothing about who entered.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::10 Workload & Machine Identity
notes.front: Secret vs identity for a service: how to tell them apart?
notes.back: A secret is something the workload has (API key, password) and must protect. An identity is something the platform proves about the workload, usually via short-lived credentials.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::10 Workload & Machine Identity
notes.front: What is the secret zero problem?
notes.back: To fetch secrets a workload needs a credential, which is itself a secret. Workload attestation breaks the loop: the platform vouches for the workload, no bootstrap secret required.
notes.analogy: You need a key to open the safe that holds the key. Attestation is the locksmith who recognises you and opens it.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::10 Workload & Machine Identity
notes.front: What does Secure Production Identity Framework for Everyone (SPIFFE) standardise?
notes.back: A naming scheme for workload identity (spiffe://trust-domain/path), credential formats (SVIDs), and the Workload API for obtaining them without secrets.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::10 Workload & Machine Identity
notes.front: What is an SVID?
notes.back: Secure Production Identity Framework for Everyone (SPIFFE) Verifiable Identity Document: a short-lived credential carrying a SPIFFE ID, either an X.509 certificate (subject alternative name (SAN) uniform resource identifier (URI)) or a JSON Web Token (JWT). The workload's proof of identity.
notes.analogy: An employee badge that expires at the end of every shift and is reissued automatically.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::10 Workload & Machine Identity
notes.front: A workload's X.509 Secure Production Identity Framework for Everyone (SPIFFE) Verifiable Identity Document (SVID) leaks. Why is the damage limited compared with a leaked static API key?
notes.back: It is short-lived and names a single workload, so it expires quickly and grants only that workload's authorizations. Rotation is automatic, not a manual clean-up.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::10 Workload & Machine Identity
notes.front: X.509-SVID vs JWT-SVID: when do you use which?
notes.back: X.509 Secure Production Identity Framework for Everyone (SPIFFE) Verifiable Identity Document (X.509-SVID) for mutual TLS (mTLS) between workloads (transport-level identity). JSON Web Token (JWT)-SVID when identity must pass through a layer that terminates TLS (Layer 7 (L7) proxies, cloud APIs).

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::10 Workload & Machine Identity
notes.front: What is workload attestation in SPIFFE Runtime Environment (SPIRE)?
notes.back: The agent inspects the calling process via platform selectors (Kubernetes pod labels/service account, Unix UID, cloud instance metadata) and matches them to a registration entry.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::10 Workload & Machine Identity
notes.text: SPIFFE Runtime Environment (SPIRE) two-step attestation: {{c1::node attestation}} proves the agent runs on a legitimate node (cloud instance identity doc, trusted platform module (TPM), k8s projected service account token (PSAT)); {{c2::workload attestation}} identifies the process calling the agent.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::10 Workload & Machine Identity
notes.front: What is a Secure Production Identity Framework for Everyone (SPIFFE) trust domain, and how does federation work between two?
notes.back: An administrative identity realm with its own certificate authority (CA) bundle. Federation exchanges bundles via the SPIFFE bundle endpoint, so workloads in domain A can verify SPIFFE Verifiable Identity Documents (SVIDs) from B.
notes.analogy: Two countries recognising each other's passports after exchanging specimen documents.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::10 Workload & Machine Identity
notes.front: How does a service mesh use workload identity for mutual TLS (mTLS)?
notes.back: The sidecar or node proxy receives an X.509 identity per workload (Secure Production Identity Framework for Everyone (SPIFFE)-formatted), authenticates peers via mTLS and feeds the peer identity into Layer 7 (L7) authorization policy.
notes.extra: Networking and Kubernetes decks cover the TLS mechanics and Istio objects; here the point is identity as the policy key.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::10 Workload & Machine Identity
notes.front: Why are projected service account tokens safer than legacy secret-based tokens in Kubernetes?
notes.back: They are time-bound, audience-bound and tied to the pod's lifetime, so a leaked token expires and only works at the intended API, not everywhere.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::10 Workload & Machine Identity
notes.front: What makes a Kubernetes service account token usable for external identity federation?
notes.back: The cluster exposes an OpenID Connect (OIDC) discovery document and JSON Web Key Set (JWKS) for its token issuer; external systems validate the JSON Web Token (JWT) like any OIDC token and map sub/aud to a trust policy.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::10 Workload & Machine Identity
notes.front: What does cloud workload identity federation exchange, mechanically?
notes.back: A platform-issued OpenID Connect (OIDC) token (Kubernetes service account (SA), GitHub Actions, another cloud) for short-lived cloud credentials, via a trust policy that pins issuer, subject and audience.
notes.extra: Pitfall: trust policies that match only on issuer let every workload in that issuer assume the role.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::10 Workload & Machine Identity
notes.front: Why is exchanging an OpenID Connect (OIDC) token for cloud credentials safer than storing a cloud key in a pipeline secret?
notes.back: The token is minted per run and short-lived, and the trust policy can pin repo, branch and audience. A stored key is static, copyable and valid from anywhere until someone rotates it.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::10 Workload & Machine Identity
notes.front: Why should a workload identity trust policy constrain sub and aud, not just iss?
notes.back: Issuer alone identifies the platform, not the workload. Any pod or pipeline from that issuer could obtain the cloud role. Subject pins the workload; audience pins the target.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::10 Workload & Machine Identity
notes.front: What is the instance metadata service risk for workload credentials?
notes.back: Any process on the node (including a compromised pod) can call the metadata endpoint and get the node's cloud credentials. Server-side request forgery (SSRF) bugs reach it too.
notes.extra: Fixes: instance metadata service version 2 (IMDSv2)-style session tokens, blocking pod access to the metadata IP, per-pod identity instead of node identity.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::10 Workload & Machine Identity
notes.front: Why is per-pod identity preferable to node identity in Kubernetes?
notes.back: Node identity is shared by every pod on the node: least privilege is impossible and audit trails blur. Per-pod identity gives each workload only its own role.
notes.analogy: Every flat with its own key, versus one key that opens the whole building.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::10 Workload & Machine Identity
notes.front: Machine identity for CI/CD: why prefer OpenID Connect (OIDC) federation over long-lived deploy keys?
notes.back: Each pipeline run gets a short-lived token asserting repo, branch and environment; cloud trust policies can require main branch only. Nothing to leak or rotate.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::11 Cloud IAM Patterns
notes.front: What is a principal in cloud identity and access management (IAM)?
notes.back: Any authenticated entity that can make a request: human user, group, service identity, federated identity or assumed role. Policies name principals.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::11 Cloud IAM Patterns
notes.front: Role vs policy in cloud identity and access management (IAM): how to keep them apart?
notes.back: A policy is the document listing allowed/denied actions on resources. A role is an assumable identity (with attached policies) that principals take on temporarily.
notes.analogy: A policy is the job description; a role is the uniform you put on to perform it.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::11 Cloud IAM Patterns
notes.front: What does assuming a role (impersonation) give you, mechanically?
notes.back: Short-lived credentials for a different identity, issued after the role's trust policy accepts you. Your permissions become the role's, not the union of both.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::11 Cloud IAM Patterns
notes.front: Trust policy vs permission policy on a role?
notes.back: Trust policy: who may assume the role. Permission policy: what the role may do. Both must allow, and the caller's own policy must also allow the assume action.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::11 Cloud IAM Patterns
notes.front: How does cross-account (cross-tenant) access work without sharing credentials?
notes.back: The target account creates a role trusting the source account's principal; the source assumes it and receives temporary credentials. Trust is declared on the resource side.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::11 Cloud IAM Patterns
notes.front: What is the confused deputy problem in cross-account roles?
notes.back: A service that assumes roles on behalf of many customers could be tricked into using customer A's role for customer B. An external ID / audience condition the caller must present prevents it.
notes.analogy: A valet with keys to many cars handed a forged ticket: the external ID is the ticket stub only the real owner has.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::11 Cloud IAM Patterns
notes.front: What is a permission boundary?
notes.back: A policy that caps the maximum permissions an identity can ever have, regardless of what is attached later. Lets teams create roles without being able to exceed the boundary.
notes.analogy: A credit limit: you choose what to buy, but the bank caps the total.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::11 Cloud IAM Patterns
notes.front: An identity has an identity policy allowing s3:* but a permission boundary that excludes s3:DeleteObject. Can it delete objects?
notes.back: No. The effective permissions are the intersection of the identity policy and the boundary: an allow must exist in both.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::11 Cloud IAM Patterns
notes.front: How do cloud providers combine identity policies, resource policies and organisation guardrails?
notes.back: Explicit deny anywhere wins; otherwise the request needs an allow from identity or resource policy, within the organisation guardrail and permission boundary.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::11 Cloud IAM Patterns
notes.front: What is privilege escalation via identity and access management (IAM), and name the generic pattern?
notes.back: Using a permitted action to gain more permissions: e.g. rights to attach policies, update a trusted role, or create credentials for a more privileged identity.
notes.extra: Classic paths: iam:PassRole + compute create; policy version update; modifying a role's trust policy; impersonating a service account.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::11 Cloud IAM Patterns
notes.front: Why is 'pass role to a service' a classic escalation primitive?
notes.back: If you may launch a workload and attach a powerful role to it, you effectively gain that role by running your own code inside the workload.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::11 Cloud IAM Patterns
notes.front: What does Just-in-Time (JIT) access change about privileged roles?
notes.back: Nobody holds admin standing. Elevation is requested, optionally approved, granted for a time window and automatically removed, with the reason logged.
notes.analogy: A tool crib: borrow the dangerous tool for the job, sign it out, sign it back in.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::11 Cloud IAM Patterns
notes.front: Standing privilege vs just-in-time (JIT) access: why does it matter for breach impact?
notes.back: A phished admin with standing privilege is an instant full compromise. With JIT, the attacker must also pass an elevation request, approval and alerting.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::11 Cloud IAM Patterns
notes.front: How should a break-glass account be designed so it's safe to exist?
notes.back: Excluded from the identity provider (IdP) dependency, phishing-resistant credential sealed offline, alert on any use, scoped and time-limited where possible, credentials rotated after each use.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::11 Cloud IAM Patterns
notes.front: Why are long-lived access keys for humans considered an anti-pattern?
notes.back: They sit in laptops, repos and CI logs for years and work from anywhere. Federated single sign-on (SSO) yields short-lived session credentials with multi-factor authentication (MFA) and central revocation.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::11 Cloud IAM Patterns
notes.front: What are service control / organisation policies for?
notes.back: Guardrails applied to whole accounts or folders that even account admins can't lift: deny regions, deny disabling logging, deny leaving the organisation.
notes.analogy: Building codes: even the owner of the house can't waive them.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::11 Cloud IAM Patterns
notes.front: What is attribute- or tag-based access control in cloud identity and access management (IAM)?
notes.back: Policies conditioned on tags of the principal and resource matching (project = ${principal.project}), so one policy scales across teams instead of one role per team.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::11 Cloud IAM Patterns
notes.front: Cross-provider concept map: AWS role, GCP service account impersonation, Azure managed identity: what do they share?
notes.back: All provide a platform-issued, short-lived credential for a workload identity without storing a secret, and all rely on a trust relationship deciding who may obtain it.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::12 Sessions, Threats & Operations
notes.front: What is a session, and why does one exist after authentication?
notes.back: A server-side (or signed) record that the user authenticated, referenced by a cookie or token, so credentials aren't re-sent on every request.
notes.analogy: A festival wristband: your ticket is checked once at the gate, then the wristband gets you through every tent.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::12 Sessions, Threats & Operations
notes.front: Server-side session vs stateless signed session (JSON Web Token (JWT) in cookie)?
notes.back: Server-side: a random ID, instantly revocable, needs a store. Stateless: self-contained, scales without shared state, can't be revoked before expiry.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::12 Sessions, Threats & Operations
notes.front: Why regenerate the session ID on login?
notes.back: Prevents session fixation: an attacker who planted a known session ID before login would otherwise own the authenticated session.
