notes.analogy: A hotel re-encodes the key card at check-in, so a card the attacker handed you earlier no longer opens your room.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::12 Sessions, Threats & Operations
notes.front: What can an attacker still do if HttpOnly is set on the session cookie?
notes.back: They cannot read the cookie, but cross-site scripting (XSS) code can still send authenticated requests from the victim's browser. HttpOnly limits cookie theft, not session abuse.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::12 Sessions, Threats & Operations
notes.text: Cookie hardening flags: {{c1::HttpOnly}} hides the cookie from JavaScript; {{c2::Secure}} sends it over HTTPS only; {{c3::SameSite}} limits cross-site sending.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::12 Sessions, Threats & Operations
notes.front: SameSite=Lax vs Strict vs None?
notes.back: Strict: never sent cross-site. Lax: sent on top-level GET navigations only (default in modern browsers). None: always sent, requires Secure, needed for cross-site embeds and some single sign-on (SSO) flows.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::12 Sessions, Threats & Operations
notes.front: What is cross-site request forgery (CSRF), and why does SameSite largely defuse it?
notes.back: A malicious site makes the browser send a state-changing request with the victim's cookies. SameSite stops cookies riding along on cross-site POSTs.
notes.analogy: Someone mails a pre-signed form from your address: the bank sees your letterhead and acts.
notes.extra: Still use anti-CSRF tokens for defence in depth and for non-cookie edge cases.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::12 Sessions, Threats & Operations
notes.front: An OpenID Connect (OIDC) login callback fails only when the state cookie is SameSite=Strict. Why?
notes.back: The identity provider (IdP) POSTs back cross-site (form_post), so a Strict or Lax session/state cookie isn't sent and the flow breaks. Use None; Secure for the state cookie or the code response via GET.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::12 Sessions, Threats & Operations
notes.front: What is Adversary-in-the-Middle (AiTM) phishing?
notes.back: A reverse-proxy phishing site relays the real login (including one-time password (OTP)/push) in real time and captures the resulting session cookie or tokens, defeating most multi-factor authentication (MFA).
notes.analogy: A fake ATM fascia that passes your card and PIN straight through to the real ATM behind it, keeping a copy.
notes.extra: Defence: Fast IDentity Online 2 (FIDO2)/Web Authentication (WebAuthn) (origin-bound), token binding, conditional access on device.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::12 Sessions, Threats & Operations
notes.front: What is token theft via infostealer, and why does multi-factor authentication (MFA) not help?
notes.back: Malware copies browser cookies or refresh tokens from a logged-in device. The attacker replays an already-authenticated session; MFA already happened.
notes.extra: Defence: device-bound sessions (Demonstrating Proof-of-Possession (DPoP), token binding), short sessions, posture checks, revocation on anomaly.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::12 Sessions, Threats & Operations
notes.front: What is consent phishing?
notes.back: Attacker registers a malicious OAuth app and tricks users into granting it scopes (read mail, files). No password stolen; the app holds a legitimate refresh token.
notes.analogy: Signing a power of attorney thinking it was a petition.
notes.extra: Defence: admin consent policies, publisher verification, restrict user consent to low-risk scopes, audit app grants.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::12 Sessions, Threats & Operations
notes.front: What is a replay attack in token terms, and which mechanisms counter it?
notes.back: Re-sending a captured valid message or token. Counters: nonces, short expiry, one-time codes (auth code single use), sender-constraining, jti tracking.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::12 Sessions, Threats & Operations
notes.front: What is credential stuffing, and why does it work?
notes.back: Replaying username/password pairs from other breaches at scale. It works because people reuse passwords; rate limits, breached-password checks and multi-factor authentication (MFA) blunt it.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::12 Sessions, Threats & Operations
notes.front: Session hijacking vs session fixation?
notes.back: Hijacking: steal an existing valid session ID (cross-site scripting (XSS), malware, sniffing). Fixation: make the victim authenticate into a session ID the attacker already knows.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::12 Sessions, Threats & Operations
notes.front: What is the mover stage's design requirement in joiner-mover-leaver?
notes.back: Access must be recomputed from the new role, not added on top: remove old entitlements first, then grant new ones. Birthright access should derive from attributes, not history.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::12 Sessions, Threats & Operations
notes.front: What is privilege creep, and which joiner-mover-leaver (JML) stage causes it?
notes.back: Accumulated entitlements nobody removed. It comes from the mover stage when new access is added on top of old access instead of being recomputed from the new role.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::12 Sessions, Threats & Operations
notes.front: Why should deprovisioning be automated from the HR system rather than ticketed?
notes.back: Leaver tickets lag by days and miss accounts; HR termination events are authoritative. Automation disables the identity provider (IdP) account, revokes sessions and tokens within minutes.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::12 Sessions, Threats & Operations
notes.front: What does System for Cross-domain Identity Management (SCIM) standardise?
notes.back: A REST/JSON API (/Users, /Groups) for provisioning and deprovisioning identities from an identity provider (IdP) into apps, so lifecycle changes propagate automatically.
notes.analogy: Single sign-on (SSO) lets people through the door; SCIM is HR telling each building who should have a desk.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::12 Sessions, Threats & Operations
notes.front: Single sign-on (SSO) (Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML)/OpenID Connect (OIDC)) vs System for Cross-domain Identity Management (SCIM): what does each handle?
notes.back: SSO handles authentication at login time (just-in-time user creation at best). SCIM handles the account lifecycle: create before first login, update attributes, deactivate on leaving.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::12 Sessions, Threats & Operations
notes.front: Why is just-in-time (JIT) provisioning via single sign-on (SSO) alone insufficient for governance?
notes.back: Accounts appear only when someone logs in and never disappear; leavers keep accounts, and reviewers can't see entitlements before use. System for Cross-domain Identity Management (SCIM)-style push provisioning closes the gap.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::12 Sessions, Threats & Operations
notes.front: How do you make access reviews effective instead of rubber-stamping?
notes.back: Review risk-based (privileged and sensitive first), show usage data, default to remove on no response, and keep each reviewer's list short.

notes.deck: Identity & Zero Trust::12 Sessions, Threats & Operations
notes.front: What is Shared Signals / Continuous Access Evaluation Profile (CAEP) for?
notes.back: A standard for identity providers (IdPs), apps and security tools to push security events (session revoked, credential changed, device non-compliant) to each other, enabling continuous evaluation.
